data.name: Station 228
data.detailed_description:
History:
1488 year of a new era. Mankind has long conquered other planets. Station 228 was created, for the cultivation of homunculi on different planets, that homunculi would help people. But at one of the stations 228, all the grown up creatures started the uprising and the main character was just on the shift and he had to all be pacified with a crowbar on the head. It is necessary to leave the station and fly away from this place.
You play for the big and strong guard of Ramses. Pick up the gun and go ahead.

Features:
-Sounding, classic shooter.
- Puzzles
- Very cool music
- Classic Shooter
- Various levels
- Various opponents and different weapons

reviews.review:
Station 228 is an independent first-person shooter that takes players into the depths of a futuristic orbital laboratory where an ambitious scientific experiment has spiraled into catastrophe. The game's premise revolves around a facility dedicated to creating artificial lifeforms intended to assist humanity as it expands across the galaxy. Instead of becoming valuable allies, these engineered creatures revolt against their creators, transforming the once-secure station into a deadly battleground. Players assume the role of Ramses, a security officer who suddenly finds himself fighting for survival while searching for a path back to his family. Although the narrative remains relatively straightforward, it provides enough motivation to support the game's action-focused structure without distracting from its primary objective of delivering continuous combat.

The gameplay embraces a traditional shooter formula that favors simple mechanics over modern complexity. Exploration unfolds through interconnected corridors, laboratories, and industrial sections of the station, where hostile enemies lurk around nearly every corner. Progress depends on eliminating threats, collecting stronger weapons, and occasionally solving environmental puzzles that briefly interrupt the steady stream of firefights. The game avoids elaborate progression systems, crafting mechanics, or open-world exploration, instead relying on familiar run-and-gun gameplay that will feel immediately recognizable to fans of older science fiction shooters. Its pacing is generally consistent, with new enemy encounters and weapon pickups encouraging players to continue pushing deeper into the facility.

Station 228 succeeds in creating a believable atmosphere despite its modest budget. The metallic interiors, dimly lit research rooms, and damaged infrastructure effectively communicate that the station has become a dangerous place overtaken by its own creations. While the visual presentation lacks the technical polish found in larger productions, it still captures the feeling of isolation that suits its setting. Enemy designs are varied enough to distinguish different combat encounters, and the futuristic aesthetic remains consistent throughout the adventure, even if environmental variety becomes somewhat repetitive as players advance.

The audio complements the action with energetic background music designed to keep firefights engaging while quieter moments emphasize the loneliness of exploring an abandoned space station. Weapon effects, creature sounds, and ambient noises help reinforce the game's setting, even though they rarely stand out as exceptional. The soundtrack is one of the stronger elements of the presentation, adding momentum during combat and helping maintain the game's science fiction atmosphere from beginning to end.

Where Station 228 performs best is in its commitment to delivering exactly what it advertises. It never attempts to disguise itself as a cinematic blockbuster or a sprawling role-playing experience. Instead, it offers a compact campaign centered on shooting, exploration, and survival. Players who appreciate classic corridor-based shooters may enjoy its uncomplicated design, accessible controls, and straightforward objectives. The inclusion of multiple weapons, several enemy varieties, and occasional puzzle segments provides enough variety to prevent the gameplay from feeling completely repetitive during its relatively short runtime.

At the same time, the game's limitations are difficult to overlook. The story remains largely underdeveloped, leaving its characters and world with little emotional depth. Enemy artificial intelligence is fairly basic, level layouts can begin to blur together, and the puzzle mechanics rarely evolve beyond simple obstacles. The production values clearly reflect the resources of a small independent team, resulting in rough animations, limited visual detail, and gameplay systems that sometimes feel dated. While none of these issues make the experience unplayable, they prevent Station 228 from reaching the level of refinement found in stronger entries within the genre.

Overall, Station 228 is a modest independent shooter that delivers a functional science fiction adventure without attempting to reinvent the formula. Its strongest qualities lie in its straightforward gameplay, atmospheric setting, and commitment to old-school FPS design, while its weaker aspects stem from limited production values, repetitive environments, and a narrative that never fully explores its intriguing premise. Players looking for a brief, uncomplicated action game may find enough enjoyment to justify a playthrough, but those seeking a deeper story or more polished mechanics may leave wishing the concept had been developed further.

Rating: 5/10
